why: After learning how LLMs work and how to engineer prompts, retrieval and evaluation around them, this module is where those pieces become autonomous systems that plan, call tools and observe results. It teaches the Thought-Action-Observation cycle once, framework-free, and then shows the same ideas in three major libraries so you can pick the right abstraction for a job. The GAIA final project and the observability bonus unit bridge directly into the production stage that follows.

Build, debug and submit an agent that scores at least 30% on the course's GAIA level-1 subset.

lessons.title: What agents are, the LLM brain, messages and special tokens
lessons.sourceRef: Unit 1 · Introduction, What is an Agent?, Quick Quiz 1, What are LLMs?, Messages and Special Tokens
lessons.summary: Unit 1 opens with Alfred the butler to define an agent as a system that uses an AI model to reason, plan and act on its environment through tools, and introduces the spectrum of agency from simple processor to multi-agent. The LLM section recaps transformers (encoder, decoder, seq2seq), next-token prediction, autoregressive decoding until the EOS token, attention and context length, with interactive tokenizer and decoding Spaces. The messages section shows that a chat is a UI abstraction: system, user and assistant messages are concatenated into one prompt by the model's chat template, which differs between SmolLM2 and Llama 3.2, and is applied with tokenizer.apply_chat_template.

concepts.def: A system that leverages an AI model to interact with its environment in order to achieve a user-defined objective, combining reasoning, planning and the execution of actions, often via tools.
Increasing levels of LLM control over program flow: simple processor, router, tool caller, multi-step agent, multi-agent.
The LLM predicts one token at a time and feeds it back as input until it emits the end-of-sequence (EOS) token.
Model-specific tokens such as <|im_end|> or <|eot_id|> that delimit sequences, turns and roles; they differ across providers.
A Jinja2 template bundled with the tokenizer that turns a list of role/content messages into the exact prompt string the model was trained on.
A base model only predicts next tokens; an instruct model is fine-tuned to follow instructions and chat, and expects its chat template.

keyPoints: An agent has a brain (the model that reasons and plans) and a body (the tools and capabilities that bound what actions are possible).
Tools and actions are not the same: an action may chain several tools.
LLMs are typically decoder-only transformers with billions of parameters whose single objective is next-token prediction; a Llama 2 vocabulary has about 32,000 tokens.
Every provider uses different EOS and delimiter tokens (GPT-4 <|endoftext|>, Llama 3 <|eot_id|>, SmolLM2 <|im_end|>, Gemma <end_of_turn>).
The model does not remember a conversation: all messages are re-sent as one prompt each turn.
The system message sets persistent behavior and, for agents, also lists the tools and the required action format.
Use tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) to render the prompt correctly for the chosen model.

lessons.title: Tools and the Thought-Action-Observation cycle
lessons.sourceRef: Unit 1 · What are Tools?, Quick Quiz 2, Thought-Action-Observation Cycle, Thought, Actions, Observe
lessons.summary: The tools page defines a tool as a function given to the LLM with a textual description, a callable, typed arguments and optional typed outputs, shows how the description is injected into the system prompt, and builds a fictional Tool class and @tool decorator that use Python introspection to generate the description automatically; it closes with a note on MCP as a unified tool interface. The cycle pages describe agents as a while loop of Thought, Action and Observation, with the Alfred weather example, then detail thought types and ReAct versus chain-of-thought, JSON versus code versus function-calling actions with the stop-and-parse approach, and how observations are appended to memory.

concepts.def: A function given to the LLM with a clear objective, described by name, description, typed arguments and output type so the model can emit a text invocation that the agent executes.
Uses inspect to read a function's name, docstring, type hints and return annotation and turn them into the tool description injected in the system prompt.
The agent loop: the LLM thinks about the next step, emits an action (tool call), the framework runs it and appends the result as an observation, repeating until a final answer.
A prompting approach that interleaves step-by-step reasoning with actions and observations; unlike chain-of-thought it uses external tools.
The LLM emits the action in a fixed format (JSON or code) and stops generating; an external parser extracts the tool and arguments and executes it.
A JSON agent specifies actions as JSON blobs; a code agent writes an executable code block, which is more expressive and composable but needs sandboxing.

keyPoints: LLMs cannot call tools themselves; the agent reads the model's text, executes the tool and appends the result as a new message before calling the model again.

Tool descriptions must be precise about what the tool does and the exact inputs it expects; the course uses the string Tool Name: calculator, Description: Multiply two integers., Arguments: a: int, b: int, Outputs: int.
Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how applications expose tools to LLMs so one tool interface works across frameworks.
Thought types include planning, analysis, decision making, self-reflection and prioritization; models fine-tuned for function calling can skip explicit thoughts.
Reasoning models such as DeepSeek R1 and OpenAI o1 wrap their reasoning in dedicated think tokens learned during training, which is a training-level technique rather than ReAct or CoT prompting.
After an action the framework parses it, executes it and appends the result as an observation; errors and status codes are observations too.
Executing LLM-generated code carries prompt-injection and harmful-code risks, so use frameworks with safeguards.

code.caption: The dummy agent loop: ReAct system prompt, stop before Observation, run the real tool, resume (adapted from Unit 1, Dummy Agent Library)
code.src:
from huggingface_hub import InferenceClient
client = InferenceClient(model="moonshotai/Kimi-K2.5", token=HF_TOKEN)
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """Answer the following questions as best you can. You have access to the following tools:
get_weather: Get the current weather in a given location, args: {"location": {"type": "string"}}
Use a json blob with an `action` key and an `action_input` key. ALWAYS use the following format:
Question: the input question you must answer
Thought: you should always think about one action to take. Only one action at a time.
Action:
$JSON_BLOB (inside markdown cell)
Observation: the result of the action. This Observation is unique, complete, and the source of truth.
... (this Thought/Action/Observation can repeat N times)
Thought: I now know the final answer
Final Answer: the final answer to the original input question"""
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in London?"}]
# stop before "Observation:" so the model cannot hallucinate the tool result
out = client.chat.completions.create(messages=messages, max_tokens=150, stop=["Observation:"])
step = out.choices[0].message.content
def get_weather(location):            # dummy tool; a real agent would call an API
    return f"the weather in {location} is sunny with low temperatures. \n"
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": step + "Observation:\n" + get_weather("London")})
final = client.chat.completions.create(messages=messages, max_tokens=200)
print(final.choices[0].message.content)   # Final Answer: The weather in London is sunny ...

lessons.title: smolagents I: code agents, tool-calling agents and tools
lessons.sourceRef: Unit 2 · Frameworks for AI Agents; Unit 2.1 · Introduction to smolagents, Why use smolagents?, Quick Quiz 1, Building Agents That Use Code, Writing actions as code snippets or JSON blobs, Tools
lessons.summary: The Unit 2 introduction lists what any agent framework must provide (LLM engine, tools, parser, synced system prompt, memory, error logging and retries) and warns that plain code is enough for simple chains. The smolagents pages present a lightweight code-first library: CodeAgent writes Python actions, ToolCallingAgent emits JSON tool calls, both are MultiStepAgents following ReAct with memory steps (SystemPromptStep, TaskStep, ActionStep). Alfred plans a Wayne Manor party: a DuckDuckGo playlist search, a suggest_menu @tool, authorized imports for datetime, pushing the agent to the Hub, and instrumenting runs with OpenTelemetry and Langfuse. The tools page covers @tool versus Tool subclasses, the default toolbox, sharing tools, loading Spaces, LangChain tools and MCP servers.

concepts.def: CodeAgent generates and executes Python snippets as actions; ToolCallingAgent uses the provider's native tool calling to emit JSON blobs that the system parses and runs.
The run is logged as a SystemPromptStep, a TaskStep and ActionSteps; write_memory_to_messages converts them to chat messages before each model call.
Wraps a typed function whose docstring has an Args section; the recommended way to define simple tools.
A class with name, description, inputs dict, output_type and a forward method, for complex tools with custom metadata or state.
The allowlist that lets the sandboxed Python executor import modules such as datetime or pandas.
Built-in tools: PythonInterpreterTool, FinalAnswerTool, UserInputTool, DuckDuckGoSearchTool, GoogleSearchTool and VisitWebpageTool.

keyPoints: smolagents is about 1,000 lines of code and favors code actions because research (Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents) shows tool-calling LLMs work better with code.
Code actions give composability, object management, generality and are natural for LLMs; JSON tool calls suit simple systems without variable handling.
InferenceClientModel defaults to Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct; other model classes are TransformersModel, LiteLLMModel, OpenAIServerModel and AzureOpenAIServerModel.
Precise allowed values in a tool docstring (casual, formal, superhero) steer the agent's arguments and limit hallucinations.
agent.push_to_hub and from_hub share and reload whole agents; shared agents are also runnable as Spaces.
Tools can be loaded from the Hub (load_tool), from a Gradio Space (Tool.from_space), from LangChain (Tool.from_langchain) or from an MCP server (ToolCollection.from_mcp).
SmolagentsInstrumentor from openinference exports every run as OpenTelemetry traces to Langfuse for debugging.

code.caption: A smolagents CodeAgent with a built-in search tool and a custom @tool (adapted from Unit 2.1, Building Agents That Use Code)
code.src:
from smolagents import CodeAgent, DuckDuckGoSearchTool, InferenceClientModel, tool
@tool
def suggest_menu(occasion: str) -> str:
    """
    Suggests a menu based on the occasion.
    Args:
        occasion: The type of occasion for the party. Allowed values are:
                  "casual", "formal", "superhero" or "custom".
    """
    if occasion == "casual":
        return "Pizza, snacks, and drinks."
    elif occasion == "formal":
        return "3-course dinner with wine and dessert."
    elif occasion == "superhero":
        return "Buffet with high-energy and healthy food."
    return "Custom menu for the butler."
agent = CodeAgent(
    tools=[DuckDuckGoSearchTool(), suggest_menu],
    model=InferenceClientModel(),                 # defaults to Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct
    additional_authorized_imports=["datetime"],   # sandboxed executor: imports must be allowlisted
    max_steps=10,
)
agent.run("Prepare a formal menu for the party and find a playlist for Wayne Manor.")
agent.push_to_hub("your-username/AlfredAgent")   # share the whole agent on the Hub

lessons.title: smolagents II: retrieval agents, multi-agent systems, vision and browser agents
lessons.sourceRef: Unit 2.1 · Retrieval Agents, Quick Quiz 2, Multi-Agent Systems, Vision and Browser agents, Final Quiz, Conclusion
lessons.summary: Retrieval agents extend RAG by letting the agent formulate queries, critique results and retrieve in several steps; the notebook builds a DuckDuckGo agent and a PartyPlanningRetrieverTool wrapping a BM25Retriever over chunked party ideas. The multi-agent page solves the Batman filming locations task: a calculate_cargo_travel_time tool, a baseline CodeAgent with planning_interval, then a web_agent managed by a DeepSeek-R1 manager with plotting imports and a final_answer_checks callback that uses a multimodal model to validate the saved map. The vision page passes images to a CodeAgent at start (Joker versus Wonder Woman) and then builds a Selenium and Helium browser agent whose step_callback saves screenshots into ActionStep.observations_images.

concepts.def: RAG where the agent controls retrieval and generation: it reformulates, decomposes or expands queries, reranks, retrieves in multiple steps and validates results.
A Tool subclass that wraps a lexical retriever over chunked documents and returns the top-k passages as the observation.
Sub-agents passed via managed_agents, each with a name and description, that a manager agent can call like tools; separate memories cut tokens and cost.
Makes the agent write an explicit plan every N steps, which helps on long multi-step tasks.
Callbacks that validate the final answer (for example a VLM judging the plot) and raise to force the agent to retry.
Functions run at the end of each step; a browser agent uses one to screenshot the page and store it on the ActionStep for the VLM.

keyPoints: Traditional RAG relies on a single similarity-based retrieval step; agentic RAG lets the agent decide when and how to retrieve again.
Enhanced strategies: query reformulation, decomposition, expansion, reranking with cross-encoders, multi-step retrieval, source integration and result validation.
Splitting a long task across a web agent and a manager keeps each agent focused and reduces input tokens per step.
manager_agent.visualize() prints the tree of agents, tools and authorized imports.
GoogleSearchTool needs a Serper or SerpAPI key; DuckDuckGoSearchTool is free but rate limited.
Vision examples require a capable VLM; the course used GPT-4o through OpenAIServerModel.
The browser agent gets tools like search_item_ctrl_f, go_back and close_popups plus helium_instructions in the task prompt.

lessons.title: LlamaIndex: components, QueryEngine tools, agents and workflows
lessons.sourceRef: Unit 2.2 · Introduction to LlamaIndex, LlamaHub, Components, Using Tools, Quick Quiz 1, Using Agents, Creating Agentic Workflows, Quick Quiz 2, Conclusion
lessons.summary: LlamaIndex is presented as a toolkit for agents over your data built from components, tools, agents and workflows, with LlamaHub as the registry (pip install llama-index-{component-type}-{framework-name}). The components notebook builds a RAG pipeline: SimpleDirectoryReader, IngestionPipeline with SentenceSplitter and HuggingFaceEmbedding into a ChromaVectorStore, VectorStoreIndex, as_query_engine with response modes, FaithfulnessEvaluator and Arize Phoenix tracing. Tools come in four kinds (FunctionTool, QueryEngineTool, ToolSpecs, utility tools, plus MCP). Agents are created with AgentWorkflow.from_tools_or_functions, remember state through Context, and combine as FunctionAgent or ReActAgent in multi-agent AgentWorkflows. Workflows chain @step functions through typed Events, support loops, branches, drawing and shared state.

concepts.def: The component that retrieves from an index and synthesizes an answer; wrapped as a QueryEngineTool it becomes a RAG tool for agents.

from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import AgentWorkflow, FunctionAgent
from llama_index.core.tools import QueryEngineTool
from llama_index.core.workflow import Context
from llama_index.llms.huggingface_api import HuggingFaceInferenceAPI
def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Multiplies two integers and returns the resulting integer"""
    return a * b

# wrap the QueryEngine built in the Components section as a RAG tool
query_engine_tool = QueryEngineTool.from_defaults(
    query_engine=index.as_query_engine(llm=llm, similarity_top_k=3),
    name="persona_db",
    description="Searches a database containing persona descriptions",
)
alfred = FunctionAgent(            # FunctionAgent needs a function-calling LLM; ReActAgent works with any LLM
    name="alfred",
    description="Answers questions using arithmetic and the persona database",
    tools=[multiply, query_engine_tool],   # plain functions are parsed for name and description
    llm=llm,
)
workflow = AgentWorkflow(agents=[alfred], root_agent="alfred")
ctx = Context(workflow)                     # keeps state and history between runs
response = await workflow.run(user_msg="What is 2 times 2?", ctx=ctx)

lessons.sourceRef: Unit 2.3 · Introduction to LangGraph, What is LangGraph?, Building Blocks, Building Your First LangGraph, Document Analysis Graph, Quick Quiz 1, Conclusion
lessons.summary: LangGraph is LangChain's framework for controlling the flow of LLM applications; it sits on the control end of the control-versus-freedom trade-off and suits multi-step processes, persisted state, deterministic logic mixed with AI, human-in-the-loop and complex architectures. Its building blocks are a user-defined State (TypedDict), Nodes (functions that return state updates), Edges (direct or conditional) and the StateGraph container compiled and invoked. The first graph is Alfred's mail sorter: read, classify spam with an LLM, route with add_conditional_edges to handle_spam or draft_response, notify, END, traced with the Langfuse CallbackHandler. The document analysis graph adds messages with the add_messages reducer, bind_tools with extract_text (a GPT-4o vision tool) and divide, a ToolNode and tools_condition to form the ReAct loop.

concepts.def: The user-defined data that flows through the graph; nodes read it and return partial updates.
A Python function that takes the state, does work such as an LLM call or tool call, and returns updates to the state.
An edge chosen at runtime by a routing function whose return value is mapped to the next node.
The builder that holds nodes and edges, starts at START, ends at END, and is compiled into a runnable graph.
An Annotated operator on a messages field that appends new messages instead of overwriting the list.
Prebuilt node that executes tool calls and prebuilt router that sends the flow to tools or END depending on whether the last message contains a tool call.

keyPoints: LangChain gives model and tool interfaces; LangGraph orchestrates control flow, and the two can be used separately.
Code agents are free and less predictable; LangGraph is for when you, the human, design the flow and let the LLM decide at junctions.

code.caption: A LangGraph StateGraph that classifies an email and routes with a conditional edge (adapted from Unit 2.3, Building Your First LangGraph)
code.src:
from typing import TypedDict, Optional, Dict, Any
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage
class EmailState(TypedDict):          # user-defined state that flows through every node
    email: Dict[str, Any]
    is_spam: Optional[bool]
    email_draft: Optional[str]
model = ChatOpenAI(temperature=0)
def classify_email(state: EmailState):   # a node reads the state and returns updates
    text = model.invoke([HumanMessage(content=f"Is this email spam or legitimate?\n{state['email']['body']}")]).content.lower()
    return {"is_spam": "spam" in text and "not spam" not in text}
def draft_response(state: EmailState):
    reply = model.invoke([HumanMessage(content=f"As Alfred the butler, draft a polite reply to: {state['email']['body']}")])
    return {"email_draft": reply.content}
def route_email(state: EmailState) -> str:   # return value must match a key of the mapping below
    return "spam" if state["is_spam"] else "legitimate"
builder = StateGraph(EmailState)
builder.add_node("classify_email", classify_email); builder.add_node("draft_response", draft_response)
builder.add_node("handle_spam", lambda state: print("Moved to the spam folder.") or {})
builder.add_edge(START, "classify_email")
builder.add_conditional_edges("classify_email", route_email, {"spam": "handle_spam", "legitimate": "draft_response"})
builder.add_edge("handle_spam", END); builder.add_edge("draft_response", END)
print(builder.compile().invoke({"email": {"body": "CONGRATULATIONS! You have won $5,000,000!"}, "is_spam": None, "email_draft": None}))

lessons.title: Bonus 1: fine-tuning an LLM for function calling with LoRA
lessons.sourceRef: Bonus Unit 1 · Introduction, What is Function Calling?, Let's Fine-Tune your model for Function-calling, Conclusion
lessons.summary: Function calling is a learned way for the model to act on its environment: instead of relying on prompting as in Unit 1, the model is fine-tuned to emit tool calls and interpret results. The unit shows how function calling adds an action and an observation to the conversation, represented through special tokens such as [AVAILABLE_TOOLS], [TOOL_CALLS] and [TOOL_RESULTS] in the Mistral chat template, and in many APIs as an assistant message with a function_call plus a tool role message. It then explains the three training stages (pre-training, instruction fine-tuning, alignment), why to start from google/gemma-2-2b-it, and LoRA, which trains small rank-decomposition adapters while freezing the base model. The notebook fine-tunes Gemma 2 2B for function calling with new special tokens that separate thinking, calls and tool responses.

concepts.def: A trained capability where the model structures its output as a call to a provided function and then reads the function result, relying less on prompting.

lessons.title: Bonus 2: agent observability and evaluation with OpenTelemetry and Langfuse
lessons.sourceRef: Bonus Unit 2 · Introduction, What is agent observability and evaluation?, Monitoring and evaluating agents, Quiz
lessons.summary: Observability means understanding an agent from logs, metrics and traces; without it agents are black boxes. Tools such as Langfuse and Arize ingest OpenTelemetry data that frameworks like smolagents expose, representing a run as a trace made of spans. Key metrics are latency, cost (token usage), request errors, explicit and implicit user feedback, accuracy and automated evaluations such as LLM-as-a-judge, RAGAS or LLM Guard. Evaluation splits into offline (curated datasets with ground truth, repeatable, for CI) and online (live traffic, drift and unexpected queries), best combined in a loop. The notebook instruments a smolagents CodeAgent with SmolagentsInstrumentor, enriches traces with user_id, session_id and tags, collects thumbs-up feedback in Gradio with langfuse.create_score, applies an LLM-as-a-judge template, and runs the agent over GSM8K items stored as a Langfuse dataset.

concepts.def: Understanding what happens inside an agent through external signals: logs, metrics and traces of actions, tool use and model calls.
A trace is one complete agent task; spans are its individual steps such as a model call or a tool call.
The open standard for instrumenting code to emit traces, metrics and logs; smolagents exposes agent metadata through it.
Offline scores the agent on curated datasets with known answers; online monitors real user interactions, feedback and drift in production.
A separate LLM scores each output against a template such as correctness or toxicity, and the score is logged to the trace.
Dataset items with input and expected output; item.run links each agent trace to the item so runs with different models or prompts can be compared.

keyPoints: Metrics to watch: latency per step and run, cost from token usage, request errors (add retries and provider fallbacks), explicit and implicit feedback, accuracy.
Repeated rephrasing or retry clicks are implicit feedback that the agent is failing.
Start with offline evaluation before deploying; keep the test set updated with new edge cases and mix small smoke sets with larger sets.
The improvement loop: offline eval, deploy, monitor online, collect failures, add them to the offline set, iterate.
span.update_trace can attach input, output, user_id, session_id, tags and metadata; call langfuse.flush() in short scripts.
If you use LlamaIndex or LangGraph, Langfuse has dedicated instrumentation docs for both.
Lines of code is not an observability metric; latency, cost and feedback are.

code.caption: Instrumenting a smolagents run with OpenTelemetry and Langfuse, then enriching the trace (adapted from Bonus Unit 2 notebook)
code.src:
import os
from langfuse import get_client
from openinference.instrumentation.smolagents import SmolagentsInstrumentor
from smolagents import CodeAgent, DuckDuckGoSearchTool, InferenceClientModel

# pip install langfuse 'smolagents[telemetry]' openinference-instrumentation-smolagents
os.environ["LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY"] = "pk-lf-..."
os.environ["LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY"] = "sk-lf-..."
os.environ["LANGFUSE_HOST"] = "https://cloud.langfuse.com"   # EU region; us.cloud.langfuse.com for US

langfuse = get_client()
assert langfuse.auth_check(), "check your Langfuse credentials"
SmolagentsInstrumentor().instrument()      # every agent run is now exported as an OpenTelemetry trace

agent = CodeAgent(tools=[DuckDuckGoSearchTool()], model=InferenceClientModel())

with langfuse.start_as_current_span(name="Smolagent-Trace") as span:
    response = agent.run("What is the capital of Germany?")
    span.update_trace(                       # attributes used later for filtering and analysis
        input="What is the capital of Germany?", output=response,
        user_id="smolagent-user-123", session_id="smolagent-session-123456789",
        tags=["city-question", "testing-agents"],
    )
langfuse.flush()                             # flush events in short-lived applications

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the role of special tokens in LLMs?
o: They are extra vocabulary words that improve text quality
They mark structure such as the end of a sequence (EOS) or the boundaries between message roles
They are random tokens inserted to increase response variability
They are only used during pre-training and removed at inference
quiz.e: Special tokens like <|im_end|> or <|eot_id|> delimit sequences and turns; chat templates insert them so each model gets the format it was trained on.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between Actions and Tools?
o: They are identical and interchangeable
Actions are the steps the agent takes; Tools are the functions it can call to perform those steps
Tools require an LLM while Actions do not
Actions are physical and Tools are digital
quiz.e: An action is what the agent does to reach its goal and may involve several tools; a tool is a specific callable described to the model.

quiz.q: In the dummy agent notebook, why is stop=["Observation:"] passed to the chat completion call?
o: To make the model answer faster
To prevent the model from fabricating the tool result so the agent can run the real function and insert its output
To stop the model from using more than one tool
To remove the Thought lines from the output
quiz.e: Without the stop sequence the model wrote its own Observation; stopping before it lets the agent execute get_weather and resume generation with the real observation.

quiz.q: How does smolagents position code-based versus JSON-based actions?
o: It only supports JSON actions and requires a parser for every call
It focuses on code actions through CodeAgent but also offers JSON tool calls through ToolCallingAgent
It forbids external function calls entirely
It requires converting every code snippet to JSON before running
quiz.e: smolagents is code-first because research shows LLMs act better in code, yet ToolCallingAgent provides the JSON alternative for simpler systems.

quiz.q: When should you subclass Tool instead of using the @tool decorator in smolagents?
o: Only for retrieval tools
Only in multi-agent systems
When you need more flexibility, custom metadata or state such as a retriever initialized in __init__
Whenever you want to skip writing a docstring
quiz.e: The decorator is recommended for simple function tools; a Tool subclass with name, description, inputs, output_type and forward suits complex tools.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of splitting the Batman locations task into a manager agent and a managed web agent?
o: It removes the need for any web search
Each agent stays focused and separate memories reduce input tokens, latency and cost
It lets the model skip planning entirely
It guarantees deterministic outputs
quiz.e: The multi-agent page shows the single agent's context filling up; the manager plus web_agent split separates memories and keeps each agent on its core task.

quiz.q: Which method keeps conversation state across calls for a LlamaIndex agent?
o: agent.run(query_str)
agent.chat(query_str, ctx=ctx)
agent.run(query_str, ctx=ctx)
agent.interact(query_str)
quiz.e: Agents are stateless by default; passing the same Context object to run preserves history and workflow state.

quiz.q: What is a conditional edge in LangGraph?
o: An edge that needs user confirmation before proceeding
An edge that is followed only when the input is valid
An edge chosen by a routing function that evaluates the current state to pick the next node
An edge that always connects START to END
quiz.e: add_conditional_edges takes a routing function whose return value is mapped to node names, creating dynamic branching from the state.

quiz.q: What is a key feature of agentic RAG as built in the gala use case?
o: It can only use document-based tools
It answers without any tools, like a chatbot
The agent can decide to use any tool, including the retriever, web search, weather or Hub stats, to answer
It only works with function-calling agents
quiz.e: Instead of always retrieving, Alfred chooses between the guest retriever, web search, weather and Hub stats tools depending on the question.

quiz.q: How does the course's Unit 4 scoring API grade your agent's answers?
o: With an LLM judge that accepts paraphrases
By exact match against the ground truth, so the submission must contain only the answer and not the text FINAL ANSWER
By keyword overlap above 50%
By human review on the leaderboard
quiz.e: The hands-on page states that /submit compares answers in an exact match manner and asks you to omit FINAL ANSWER; 30% or higher earns the certificate.

quiz.q: What does function calling change in the conversation structure compared with the plain user/assistant exchange?
o: Nothing; tool calls are hidden in the system prompt
It adds an action (the assistant's function_call) and an observation (a tool role message), represented by special tokens in the chat template
It replaces the assistant role with a tool role
It removes the need for a system message
quiz.e: The Mistral example shows an assistant message with function_call followed by a tool message, rendered with tokens like [TOOL_CALLS] and [TOOL_RESULTS].

quiz.q: What best describes offline evaluation of an AI agent?
o: Evaluating the agent on real user interactions in production
Assessing performance on curated datasets with known ground truth before or during development
Monitoring internal logs in real time
Running the agent without any metrics
quiz.e: Offline evaluation uses test sets such as GSM8K with expected answers; it is repeatable and the minimum step before deploying, complemented by online evaluation.

project.title: Build, trace and submit a GAIA level-1 agent
project.brief: Starting from the Final_Assignment_Template Space, build an agent in the framework of your choice that answers the course's 20 GAIA level-1 questions through the scoring API. Equip it with web search, page reading, Python execution and file tools, add retries and a strict final-answer formatter, instrument it with OpenTelemetry and Langfuse, and iterate on traces until it scores 30% or higher on the student leaderboard.
steps: Duplicate the Final_Assignment_Template Space, add your HF_TOKEN and run the baseline to understand the questions, attached files and the answers payload.
Choose smolagents, LlamaIndex or LangGraph and build the agent with web search, visit webpage, a Python interpreter and readers for the file types present in the questions.
Add retries with backoff around tool and model calls and a max_steps or iteration budget per question.
Write an answer-formatting step that returns only the final value: no explanations, correct units, lists and plural forms, and never the text FINAL ANSWER.
Instrument the agent with SmolagentsInstrumentor or the Langfuse LlamaIndex or LangGraph integration and tag each trace with the task_id.
Run all 20 questions, classify failures from the traces (retrieval, reasoning, formatting, tool error) and fix the largest category first.
Submit from your public Space, verify your entry on the Students leaderboard and claim the certificate once you reach 30% or higher.
Write a short README describing the tool set, the failure analysis and the final score.

rubric.meets: The agent has search, browsing, code execution and file tools wired into a documented agent loop in one framework, with a clear system prompt.
Tool and model errors are retried with backoff, every question has a step budget, and the agent never crashes the full run.
Submitted answers contain only the value, obey the question's format (units, list order, plurals) and never include FINAL ANSWER.
Every question's run is a trace tagged with its task_id, and the README cites at least three traces used to fix failures.
The public Space scores 30% or higher on the leaderboard and another student can rerun it with only an HF token.

stretch: Add a manager plus web-agent multi-agent structure and compare score, cost and latency with the single agent.
Build an offline evaluation dataset in Langfuse from the 20 questions and compare two models or prompts side by side.
Expose your best tools through an MCP server and load them with ToolCollection.from_mcp or McpToolSpec.

glossary.def: A system using an AI model to reason, plan and act on its environment through tools to achieve a user-defined objective.
The range from simple processor to router, tool caller, multi-step agent and multi-agent, by how much the LLM controls program flow.
The tokenizer's Jinja2 template that turns messages into a prompt with the model's special tokens.
Model-specific tokens such as EOS and role delimiters that structure prompts and generations.
The agent loop of reasoning, emitting a tool call, and reading the tool result, repeated until a final answer.
Prompting that interleaves reasoning steps with actions and observations.
Generating an action in a fixed format, halting generation, then parsing and executing it.
smolagents agent whose actions are Python snippets executed in a sandbox with an import allowlist.
smolagents agent that emits JSON tool calls through the model provider's tool-calling API.
A smolagents sub-agent with a name and description that a manager agent can delegate to.
LlamaIndex component that retrieves from an index and synthesizes an answer; wrapped as QueryEngineTool for agents.
LlamaIndex runner for one or more FunctionAgent or ReActAgent instances with a root agent and optional shared state.
A typed message that triggers a @step in a LlamaIndex Workflow; StartEvent and StopEvent bound the run.
LangGraph builder holding a typed state, nodes and edges that is compiled into an invokable graph.
A LangGraph edge whose target is chosen by a routing function evaluating the state.
LangGraph prebuilt node that executes tool calls and router that loops to it while the model keeps calling tools.
Retrieval-augmented generation where the agent controls when and how to retrieve, reformulate, rerank and validate.
Benchmark of 466 real-world assistant questions in three levels, scored by exact match; the course uses 20 level-1 items.
A trained capability to emit structured tool calls and read tool results, encoded with dedicated roles and special tokens.
Observability units: a trace is a full agent run, a span is one step inside it, exported via OpenTelemetry.
